newsitem.title: USA: Sept U.S PPI may contain seeds of higher inflation.
newsitem.headline: Sept U.S PPI may contain seeds of higher inflation.

text.p: Price stirrings at the earliest stages of production suggest the U.S. economy will endure at least modestly higher inflation in coming months, analysts said on Friday.

While the September producer price index (PPI) report showed little change in the recent trend of low finished goods inflation, crude and intermediate goods prices are rising at a troubling pace, analysts said.
"That serves as a reminder that this is no time to get complacent about inflation risks," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc.
The Labor Department reported overall PPI rose 0.2 percent in September, while the core rate, excluding food and energy inputs, rose 0.3 percent.
That approximated consensus forecasts in a Reuters poll for gains of 0.3 percent overall and 0.2 percent on the core.
The modest core rate overshoot grew out of a surprising 1.2-percent gain in passenger car prices, which reflected disappointingly small discounts at the end of the model year, analysts said.
"If you take out motor vehicles from the core rate, inflation looks very calm," said Russell Sheldon, senior economist at Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh.
Core PPI has risen only 1.4 percent over the 12 months ending in September, while the overall PPI has climbed 2.9 percent.
Analysts played down the overall increase, citing unsustainable gains in food and energy prices. Heating oil prices have risen 25.3 percent year-over-year, while gasoline prices are up 14.2 percent.

While those kinds of inflation omens could trouble the inflation fighters at the Federal Reserve, analysts said the data are unlikely to push the central bank to tighten credit at the November 13 Federal Open Market Committee meeting.
"Food and energy prices could easily go the other way next year. It's not the kind of thing we need a policy reaction to," Sheldon said.

Cary Leahey, senior financial markets economist at Lehman Government Securities, said, "What is troublesome is the apparent bottoming in inflation. The long disinflation in producer prices that began in early 1995 seems to be over."
Fortunately, the U.S. economy appears to be slowing from the second quarter of 1996, which saw a robust 4.7 percent rise in gross domestic product, analysts said.
That should rein in inflation, preserving the Fed's stellar recent performance in preserving non-inflationary growth, analysts said.

"The Fed looks like they were quite right to wait for information that would show the economy picking up in the fourth quarter before tightening. The third quarter looks pretty soft right now," Berner said.
Any uptick in inflation will likely top out well below historical cyclical peaks, analysts noted.
"We may have hit the low for the cycle, but the good news is if we do get an inflation increase, it won't be as high as in the past, maybe about one percent" higher from current levels, Leahey said.
